summary.text: Lesson 1-2 of enVision Math Grade 4: how neighbouring places relate. A digit one place to the left is worth ten times as much; one place to the right is worth one-tenth as much. Covers digit values, comparing the same digit in different places, and times-ten and divide-by-ten problems.

why.text: Every lesson after this one leans on the ten-times staircase — comparing, rounding, and eventually multiplying and dividing by tens all come back to this single picture. Get the staircase and the rest of the topic is walking it.

objectives.text: State how a digit's value changes one place left or right
Find the value of any digit in a number up to one million
Compare the values of the same digit in two different places
Solve times-ten and divide-by-ten problems with the place-value slide

parentNote.text: Built from the HW 1-2 sheet in her Drive folder. Every question is fresh — the sheet stays her homework. The one confusion this lesson exists to remove: two identical digits do NOT have the same value unless they share a place (the sheet's own 5,555 question is about exactly this, and two questions here work it). One-sitting quiz of 10 per the new lesson-a-day format.

nextUp.text: Cards, then the quiz in one sitting. If the two-7s question is easy, this lesson is in.

cards.def:
**A digit one place to the LEFT is worth ten times as much.**
• 10 is ten times 1, 100 is ten times 10, 1,000 is ten times 100.
• That is the whole design of our number system: each place is a ten-times step.

**A digit one place to the RIGHT is worth one-tenth as much.**
• 100 is one-tenth of 1,000.
• Same staircase as ten-times, walked the other direction.
cards.hint: Left is times ten. Right is divide by ten. One staircase, two directions.

cards.def:
**A digit's value is the digit times its place.**
• In 23,406 the 3 is in the thousands place, so its value is 3,000.
• The 4 is in the hundreds place, so its value is 400.

**The same digit two places apart differs in value by 100 times, not 10.**
• In 44,492 the first 4 is worth 40,000 and the second is worth 4,000 — ten times apart.
• The third 4 is worth 400 — a hundred times less than the first.
cards.hint: Count the places between the digits. Each place is one more factor of ten.

cards.term: The digits are not the values
cards.def:
**Two 5s in one number never have the same value unless they share a place.**
• In 5,555 the digits are identical but the values are 5,000, 500, 50 and 5.
• Saying the digits are equal is true; saying the values are equal is the classic mistake.

questions.q: In 68,517, what is the value of the 8?
questions.hint: Name the place first, then multiply.
steps: Read the places from the right: 7 ones, 1 ten, 5 hundreds, 8 thousands, 6 ten thousands.
The 8 sits in the thousands place.
So its value is 8 × 1,000 = 8,000.

ex.main: **8,000.** The digit only tells you WHICH number of that place you have — the place supplies the size.
ex.tip: Say the number aloud: sixty-eight thousand… you can hear the 8 living in the thousands.

questions.q: 1,000 is how many times as much as 100?
opts: 10 times
100 times
2 times
1,000 times
questions.hint: How many hundreds fit inside a thousand?
steps: Count up: 100, 200, 300 … 1,000 takes ten steps.
So ten hundreds make one thousand.
1,000 is 10 times as much as 100.

ex.main: **10 times.** Every neighbouring pair of places has this exact relationship.
ex.tip: This never changes as numbers grow: a million is ten times a hundred thousand, too.

questions.hint: One-tenth means one place to the right.
steps: One-tenth of a number is that number divided by 10.
Check backwards: 4,000 × 10 = 40,000. It fits.

ex.main: **4,000.** The 4 slides one place to the right and its value drops by a factor of ten.
ex.tip: The backwards check (multiply by 10) catches almost every slip on these.

questions.q: A charity collects 6,000 cans and shares them equally among 10 food banks. How many cans does each food bank get?
questions.hint: Sharing equally among 10 is dividing by 10.
steps: Equal shares among 10 means 6,000 ÷ 10.
Dividing by ten moves the value one place to the right: 6,000 becomes 600.
Check: 600 × 10 = 6,000. Every can is accounted for.

ex.main: **600.** Dividing by ten is a place-value slide, not a long-division job.
ex.tip: Whenever the divider is exactly 10, look for the slide instead of computing.

questions.q: A school library has 90 atlases and ten times as many novels. How many novels does it have?
questions.hint: Ten times as many means multiply by ten.
steps: Ten times as many novels as 90 atlases is 90 × 10.
Multiplying by ten slides the value one place left: 90 becomes 900.
So the library has 900 novels.

ex.main: **900.** "Ten times as many" is the phrase this whole lesson lives inside.
ex.tip: Adding ten (100) and ten TIMES (900) are very different — the word "times" is the signal.

questions.q: In 77,215, how does the value of the first 7 compare to the value of the second 7?
opts: It is ten times as great
It is one hundred times as great
They are equal
It is one-tenth as great
questions.hint: The two 7s sit in neighbouring places.
steps: The first 7 is in the ten thousands place: value 70,000.
The second 7 is in the thousands place: value 7,000.
70,000 is ten times 7,000, so the first is ten times as great.

ex.main: **Ten times as great.** Neighbouring places always differ by a factor of exactly ten.
ex.tip: Write the two values out before comparing. The places do the work for you.

questions.q: Write a number where the 6 is worth ten times as much as the 6 in 236,894. Which works?
questions.hint: Find the value of the 6 first, then find a number where a 6 is worth ten times that.
steps: In 236,894 the 6 sits in the thousands place, so it is worth 6,000.
Ten times 6,000 is 60,000 — you need a 6 in the ten thousands place.
In 261,000 the 6 is in the ten thousands place: worth 60,000. That works.
In the others, the 6 is worth 6,000, 600 or 20 — none is 60,000.

ex.main: **261,000.** The question is really "put a 6 in the ten thousands place", once you translate it.
ex.tip: Translate value questions into place questions. Places are easier to see than values.

questions.q: A student says that in 3,533, the two 3s have the same value because they are the same digit. What is the best correction?
opts: The digits match but the places differ — one 3 is worth 3,000 and the other is worth 3
The student is right, digits always keep their value
The 3s are worth 300 each
Only the 5 has a value in this number
questions.hint: Digit and value are different things. Where does each 3 sit?
steps: The first 3 is in the thousands place: value 3,000.
The last 3 is in the ones place: value 3.
Same digit, different places — the values differ by a factor of 1,000.
A digit has no size of its own until a place gives it one.

ex.main: **Same digit, different places, different values.** This is the exact confusion the lesson is built to remove.
ex.tip: When you hear "same digit", immediately ask "same place?" If not, the values differ.

questions.q: In 55,055, the two 5s at the front are next to each other, and so are the two 5s at the back. Is the relationship between each pair the same?
opts: Yes — in each pair, the left 5 is worth ten times the right 5
No — the front pair differs by ten times, the back pair by one hundred
No — only the front pair are related
Yes — all four 5s have equal value
questions.hint: Work out all four values, then compare within each pair.
steps: Front pair: 50,000 and 5,000 — the left is ten times the right.
Back pair: 50 and 5 — the left is ten times the right.
Both pairs are neighbours, so both step by a factor of ten.
The SIZES differ between pairs, but the relationship inside each pair is identical.

ex.main: **Yes — each left neighbour is worth ten times its right neighbour.** The ten-times rule holds anywhere in the number, big places or small.
ex.tip: This is the deep fact of the lesson: the rule does not care where in the number you stand.

questions.q: A game doubles your points every level, starting at 2,000. A different game multiplies points by ten each level, starting at 2,000. After one level, how do the two scores compare?
opts: 4,000 versus 20,000 — the ten-times game gives five times as much
Both give 20,000
Both give 4,000
questions.hint: Work each game out separately, then compare.
steps: Doubling 2,000 gives 4,000.
Ten times 2,000 gives 20,000 — the value slides one whole place left.
Compare: 20,000 ÷ 4,000 = 5, so the ten-times game gives five times as much after one level.

ex.main: **4,000 versus 20,000.** Times ten is a place-value jump; doubling is not — keeping those separate is real number sense.
ex.tip: A place-value slide beats a double every time. That gap only grows with more levels.
